key_terms.meaning: Q = energy stored ÷ energy lost per radian; high Q gives narrow, low-loss resonators.
A reverse-biased diode used as a voltage-tuned capacitor; capacitance falls as reverse bias rises.
NF = 10 log₁₀(F), where F = SNRin ÷ SNRout for a matched source at 290 K.
Ftotal = F1 + (F2−1)/G1 + (F3−1)/(G1G2) + …; first-stage gain suppresses later noise.
Pin,min = −174 dBm/Hz + NF + 10 log₁₀B + SNRmin, the weakest signal for the required SNR.
Input power where amplifier gain falls by 1 dB from its small-signal value; written P1dB.
Input third-order intercept: extrapolated input power where third-order IM equals the fundamental.
Spurious-free dynamic range: range from noise floor to the power where IM3 equals the noise floor.
Receiver that mixes RF to an intermediate frequency (IF), filters at IF, then demodulates.
fimage = 2fLO − fRF; it also lands at the same IF and must be filtered.
Zero-IF receiver: LO frequency equals RF, so mixing gives baseband I and Q directly.
Two mixers with quadrature LO and IF combining that cancel one sideband (image).
Frequency-selective network that shares one antenna between transmitter and receiver.
Allowed transmitter power versus frequency offset from the carrier; limits splatter into nearby channels.
Low-noise amplifier: first gain stage, sets receiver noise figure and must stay linear.
Mixer output signal power ÷ input signal power at the wanted sideband, in dB.
Power-added efficiency = (Pout − Pin)/Pdc × 100%; includes RF drive power.
Single-sideband noise power in 1 Hz at offset Δf divided by carrier power, written L(Δf) in dBc/Hz.
Oscillation needs loop gain |Aβ| ≥ 1 and loop phase shift 0° (or 360°) at the wanted frequency.
PLL bandwidth that trades fast tuning against suppression of reference and VCO phase noise.

takeaways: Passive RF parts carry Q, parasitics and tuning limits; choose them before blaming the circuit.
Noise figure is SNR loss; the cascade formula shows the first stage and its gain set receiver noise.
Sensitivity is noise floor plus NF plus bandwidth plus required SNR.
Nonlinearity sets P1dB and IIP3; SFDR is the usable range between noise and distortion.
Superheterodyne wins selectivity and image filtering but needs an image filter and IF stages.
Direct conversion removes the image and IF filter but fights DC offset, flicker noise and I/Q mismatch.
LNA design is a noise match, gain, linearity and stability compromise.
A mixer is a multiplier; conversion gain, isolation and spurs decide up-conversion and down-conversion.
PA classes trade conduction angle and efficiency against linearity; linearization protects the spectral mask.
An oscillator needs loop gain and zero phase; phase noise and PLL bandwidth set spectral purity.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask you to draw the block diagram, write the defining formula with units, and trade noise, linearity, image and efficiency against one another.

bank.q: Define noise figure, cascaded noise factor and sensitivity. Write the Friis formula for three stages and explain why the first stage dominates.
outline: Friis formula with F1, G1, F2, G2, F3
sensitivity equation and meaning of each term

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a superheterodyne receiver and explain the role of the RF filter, mixer, IF filter and demodulator. Define image frequency.
List PA classes A, B, AB and C. For each give conduction angle, approximate maximum efficiency and linearity.
outline: class AB between A and B
class C below 180°, high efficiency, poor linearity

bank.q: State the Barkhausen criterion. Explain how a VCO tunes frequency and what phase noise means in the frequency domain.
outline: phase noise as dBc/Hz at offset

bank.q: A receiver has LNA gain 15 dB, NF 2 dB; mixer gain 10 dB, NF 8 dB; IF amplifier gain 20 dB, NF 6 dB. Convert to linear and compute total noise figure in dB.
outline: convert dB to linear G and F
compute and convert back to dB

bank.q: An amplifier has IIP3 = −10 dBm and gain = 20 dB. Find OIP3. For NF = 6 dB and bandwidth = 1 MHz, write the SFDR expression and compute its value for the usual two-tone formula.
A mixer has RF = 2.1 GHz and LO = 1.8 GHz. Find the wanted IF for down-conversion, the image frequency, and the LO for up-conversion to 2.1 GHz.
outline: up-conversion uses sum or difference frequency

bank.q: A PA delivers 30 dBm RF output with 10 W DC input and 0.5 W RF drive. Compute drain efficiency and PAE. Comment on heat.
A direct-conversion receiver uses a 2.4 GHz LO. List three mechanisms that put unwanted energy at DC and explain one fix for each.
outline: fixes include isolation, differential design and offset calibration

bank.q: Compare superheterodyne, direct-conversion and image-reject receivers on image rejection, DC offset, selectivity and power. Recommend one for a low-cost narrowband sensor.
outline: superhet: good selectivity, needs image filter and IF SAW
direct conversion: no image, DC/flicker/IQ problems
image reject: RC/quadrature matching limits IRR

bank.q: Analyze how LNA noise figure, gain and IIP3 together set receiver sensitivity and blocking performance. Use Friis and a two-stage example.
outline: high gain lowers later NF but lowers input-referred IIP3

bank.q: Evaluate three linearization methods for a PA: back-off, digital predistortion and feedforward. Relate each to spectral mask, efficiency and complexity.
outline: DPD improves linearity with digital cost
feedforward wideband but complex and inefficient

bank.q: Evaluate phase noise and PLL loop bandwidth trade-offs in a synthesizer for a receiver that must reject a strong nearby blocker. Include reciprocal mixing and tuning time.
outline: narrow loop filters VCO noise but slows tuning
wide loop follows reference and is faster

glossary.def: A logarithmic ratio: 10 log₁₀(P2/P1) for power and 20 log₁₀(V2/V1) for voltage.
Power in dB relative to 1 mW: P(dBm) = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW).
Signal power lost when a part is inserted, usually positive dB when the output is smaller.
Ratio in dB of incident power to reflected power at a port; a larger value means a better match.
Making source and load impedances conjugately equal so power transfer is maximum and reflection is low.
Unwanted capacitance between device terminals or layout nodes that limits RF bandwidth and tuning.
A diode used as a variable capacitor whose junction capacitance changes with reverse bias.
F = SNRin/SNRout for a matched source, a linear ratio used in cascaded noise calculations.
NF = 10 log₁₀(F), the SNR degradation of a stage in dB.
Total noise factor from Friis formula, dominated by the first stage when its gain is high.
Minimum input signal that gives the required output SNR under stated bandwidth and NF.
Reduction of small-signal gain at high input power; P1dB is the 1 dB drop point.
Distortion products created when two or more tones pass through a nonlinear device.
Input third-order intercept point, an extrapolated power level for comparing third-order linearity.
Spurious-free dynamic range between the noise floor and the level where third-order distortion reaches it.
Receiver type that converts RF to a fixed IF for filtering and gain before demodulation.
Unwanted input frequency that mixes to the same IF as the wanted RF, fimage = 2fLO − fRF.
Zero-IF receiver that mixes RF straight to baseband, avoiding an image but facing DC offset.
Architecture or mixer that cancels the image by quadrature combining, limited by gain and phase mismatch.
Filter network that lets a transmitter and receiver share an antenna without mutual interference.
Low-noise amplifier placed first in a receiver to add gain with little added noise.
Device that multiplies RF and LO signals to translate frequency up or down.
Ratio in dB of wanted output signal power to input signal power for a mixer.
Power-added efficiency: (Pout − Pin)/Pdc × 100%, the RF output improvement per DC input.
Spectral spreading around an oscillator carrier, measured in dBc/Hz at a frequency offset.
Phase-locked loop that locks a VCO to a reference and sets synthesizer frequency and noise.
